definition: Interminable means seeming to have no end.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word interminable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know interminable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The toddler judged the checkout line interminable and said so, at volume, in the only word he had: 'Done.'
A drawn-out speech runs long and everyone feels it; interminable turns the complaint all the way up — it seems to have no end at all.
Everlasting outruns interminable: the interminable assembly does eventually end — it only feels endless — while the everlasting flame truly never goes out.

Endless is the plain twin, and read literally it makes a bigger claim than interminable: truly without end. In everyday complaint the two swap freely, but interminable keeps a wink of honesty built in — the thing does end; it only behaves as if it never will.

Never-ending is the everyday overstatement, first cousin to a groan — the never-ending meeting, the never-ending roadwork. Interminable files the same complaint in longer trousers: formal, faintly comic, and honest underneath, since the interminable thing does eventually terminate.

The eighth-grade awards night was scheduled for one hour.
There were certificates for attendance, for improved attendance, for very nearly perfect attendance; a slideshow; then a second slideshow correcting the first.
Somewhere past the ninety-minute mark, time stopped behaving — parents swore the clock's hands were painted on.
The evening was, in the only word for it, interminable.
Interminable measures the feel of time, not the fact of it: the evening did end, as evenings do.
That is the word's little joke — in- + terminus, 'no end,' filed as a complaint against things that merely end too slowly.
When something literally cannot end, everlasting makes the factual claim; interminable just rolls its eyes.
Interminable files a complaint about felt time: the meeting, speech, or layover that outlives the sitting.
It ends — it just doesn't seem to.
For things that literally never end, everlasting makes the factual claim; interminable is the eye-roll, so don't spend it on anything you enjoyed.

The minutes of the Millbrook Traffic Advisory Committee for March 4th run to forty-one pages, and they record a municipal legend: the stop-sign meeting.

Convened at six to decide whether Cedar Lane needed a second stop sign, the session heard every resident of the street, two engineers, a retired judge with a slideshow, and one man who had simply been unable to find parking.
Attendees describe the evening as interminable.
The chairwoman's own notes, written at the two-hundred-minute mark, read simply: 'No stopping point anywhere in sight.' Yet stop it did, at 11:47, with a vote of nine to nothing in favor of the sign.
The committee has since adopted a two-hour limit, printed at the top of every agenda in bold.
